Criticising all political parties is important, and nobody should be above scrutiny. author: @harshkumar-pi2yg
text:
Sarthak bhai, I regularly watch all your Sunday Show videos, and most of the time, I agree with the points you make. However, regarding your point about the Raksha Bandhan ad, I don't think I completely agree with your perspective.
In my opinion, the boy/brother shown in the ad is wearing ethnic clothing traditionally associated with Raksha Bandhan—proper kurta and pyjama. He isn't wearing shorts or anything inappropriate. So my question is: why should we sexualize or overanalyse the clothes of the woman in a traditional setting? I don't think there is any need for that.
Personally, I have no problem with a woman wearing whatever she wants. If someone wants to wear a bikini or any other type of clothing at a party or elsewhere, that's their personal choice. But when it comes to traditional festivals, religious places, or cultural occasions, I feel it is reasonable to expect clothing that reflects the tradition and the occasion.
I completely agree that ultimately, what someone wears is their personal choice. But an advertisement is created for a general audience, and the creators usually try to make it relatable to the majority of people. Raksha Bandhan is traditionally a festival celebrating the bond between a brother and sister, and for many people, it is also a culturally significant and sacred occasion. Generally, brothers and sisters wouldn't dress in or perceive each other through clothing that might be considered more revealing in such a context. So I personally don't understand why the advertisement chose to portray it that way.
I don't have a problem with the same kind of clothing being shown in movies, parties, or other contexts. My point is specifically about the setting and the occasion. When you're portraying a traditional festival or cultural practice, I feel the advertisement should respect and reflect the cultural context.
That's just my personal opinion. I respect that others may see it differently, but I felt the ad wasn't particularly appropriate for a Raksha Bandhan-themed advertisement.

author: @AyanSohail-oq7vk
text:
My POV on the burqa/hijab: I don't think it's fair to automatically call hijab or burqa “patriarchal” or oppressive just because a woman covers her body. In Islam, modesty and veiling come from religious teachings, and many Muslim women genuinely choose hijab because they believe it is a religious obligation and part of their faith.

I also think we need to separate personal choice from legal enforcement. If a woman willingly wears hijab because she believes Allah has commanded it, that is a religious choice. But if a state legally forces her to wear it, then she does not have unrestricted freedom of dress. I can personally believe in Sharia-based governance while still acknowledging that such a system places legal restrictions on individual choices in public.

What I disagree with is the idea that women's empowerment should be measured by how much of their body they can reveal. To me, real empowerment is being educated, working, earning, creating, making decisions, and being valued for your intelligence and abilities rather than primarily for your appearance.

Attention is also not the same as empowerment. A woman receiving more attention because of her body does not automatically mean she has more power. Research on sexual objectification shows that reducing women to appearance or sexual attractiveness can affect how their competence is perceived.

So I don't think the issue should be “hijab = oppression” or “revealing clothes = empowerment.” A woman wearing hijab isn't automatically oppressed, just as a woman who doesn't wear it isn't automatically empowered. We should be careful not to define a woman's freedom or value by how much of her body she shows.

I wanted to put out this opinion about that Apoorva Makhija thing you said. Although pehli cheez naa mujhe uski existence aur naa use meri existence se farak padega.

But I've been thinking about this whole women empowerment thing lately. First off, let me be clear I do support equal rights, equal opportunities and wherever whoever is best must get the opportunity to perform.

And feminism was started by professors and learned people of their own time in 1970s from what I know about, but lately I don't know from when it has been hijacked by stupid people who have equated freedom = sexual representation only. Somehow, it all feels the same to me now. I could be wrong, yes, but the "influencers" who say You Go Girl and all those things without talking about the nitty gritties of situation that what they are talking about is even right or wrong bothers me a lot. The other day, I saw a video of the mentioned Rebel Kid saying in some interview that if men are stupid enough to pay, you should monetize your sexuality. And yes, one can argue that she is correct, par behen(and not just her) hazaaro careers hain, ye sab hi kyun baar baar sunne ko milta rehta hai kuch naa kuch sexuality related, either via some influencers or media/shows/TV ki bas ye karlo life jhingalala. And audience should try to understand this as well, agar wo normal baatein karegi ya koi bhi so called influencer kuch shocking nahin bolega to views nahin aayenge aur ghar nahin chalega unka, wo baat alag hai ki wo influencer kisi businessman/rich person ka beta/beti ho. Their job is to influence to make money, isiliye imo we should try(cannot 100% succeed, kyunki insaan ho) to collect honest information (jaise sarthak bhaai ke show se 😁😅) and make our own opinions most of the time.

That's why imo, You Go Girl bina samjhe ki wo cheez larger context/long term mein sahi hai ya galat nahin bolna chahiye, warna aise to You Go Boy bolke domestic violence ko badhawa dete aayein hain log aaj tak.

And I get the character assassination part, jab sahi mein koi 2 kaudi ke vyakti ko kisi successful aurat ko neecha dikhaana hota hai to they go on their character which is utterly wrong and I myself condemn it and it shouldn't happen.

But why something always relating to clothes, sexuality and this stupid non sense. The first programmer was a woman, Madam Curie was a great scientist, aisi cheezon ke baare mein mainstream mein baat kyun nahin hua karti 80-90% of the time ki ladkiyaan aage badhe aur badh chadhkar bhaag le in sab cheezon mein. Sports ho gaye, academics ho gaya aur kai cheezein hai.

This is more of a rant which I've felt regarding this female empowerment always getting somehow related to, in a highlighted manner, to sexuality and freedom of wearing clothes and shit. Par ho ye bhi sakta hai ki meri feed hi faaltu ho, although I refrain from watching female empowerment content altogether to keep my mind sane and believe in real equality for women in any field and not go into that factory of brainwashing ki bas freedom matlab sexualise hona. They are humans too and have a lot of aspects to their lives. And for the ones which actually matter, we must fight for it and get them the rights.

There are 3 major problems with this idea: 
1. The promotion of scientists will bring them fame which may act as a distraction from their core work. Some scientists may not be wanting the limelight of the society and rather focus on their work but media will start chasing them.
2. It will bring animosity between scientists as some will get recognition while others may not
3. The idea of becoming a scientist will shift from nation building to getting listed on the LED board and for that they will start focusing on pleasing their political masters rather than doing actual research work.
To conclude, while it is important to recognise efforts of out scientists which we can achieve through awards, making movies/series on them, publishing their contribution in the books to motivate kids, school visits, etc.

author: @witharyan1
text:
In India, there is still a serious lack of respect and recognition for both scientists and teachers. I completely agree that scientists are the backbone of a country’s development, innovation, and progress. But we often forget that behind every scientist is a teacher who helped shape their knowledge, curiosity, discipline, and ambition.
Teachers are the builders of the scientists, engineers, doctors, researchers, and leaders of tomorrow. Yet, instead of allowing them to focus on education, we often see teachers being assigned duties such as census work, BLO duties, elections, surveys, and various other administrative responsibilities.

This raises an important question: How serious are we really about building the future of our country?

If we want India to become a global leader in science, technology, and innovation, we must first strengthen the foundation — our education system and our teachers. Teachers should be given the time, resources, respect, and freedom to teach. Administrative responsibilities that have little to do with education should not come at the cost of students’ learning.

A country cannot build a strong scientific community without first building a strong educational foundation. If scientists are the backbone of national development, teachers are the hands that shape that backbone.
Investing in teachers is, ultimately, an investment in India’s scientific and technological future.

author: @jainampatel2030
text:
What China has achieved is undeniably something the rest of the world can learn from—there’s no question about that. But what I find far more interesting is the timing and the narrative surrounding it.
At one moment, the world was watching China face serious criticism over the censorship of information surrounding the Nepal floods and the apparent manipulation of algorithms to protect its own interests. Then, almost overnight, the narrative seemed to shift—social media was suddenly flooded with content celebrating China’s scientists, technological achievements, and national progress.
Maybe it’s just a coincidence. But when the information environment changes this dramatically and this quickly, it’s worth asking whether we’re simply witnessing organic public interest—or a carefully managed narrative.
That contrast is what I find strange. The question isn’t whether China has achieved remarkable things—it clearly has. The question is: who controls the narrative, and how much of what we see is actually organic

वैज्ञानिकों को बोर्ड/निर्णयकारी संस्थाओं में शामिल किया जाना चाहिए, क्योंकि इससे वैज्ञानिक दृष्टिकोण, तकनीकी विशेषज्ञता और evidence-based policy making को बढ़ावा मिलेगा।

author: @victorrichard
text:
Sorry to hear you losing your photos with iCloud backup, but that really wasn’t the iPhones fault. I learnt years ago to not back up your photos (or any important data storage items) to one specific storage type (especially one you are not subscribed to). About 15 years ago I lost a couple thousand digital photos to a failed hard drive on my MacBook. It wasn’t the MacBooks fault, it was my then 8 year old son who was curious what would happen when you put a magnet near a MacBook Hard Drive. Not to worry I thought. I also had them backed up on my HP laptop. Unfortunately my son was really curious and tried that computer first. After that, I learned to back up to external sources (I now back up to two separate external SSD drives and Amazon Photo (for the photos at least. Backs up photos  at full resolution). My son (who is also older and wiser) and I are also on the process of building a NAS.
I was able to recover a good chunk of the photos (about 40%) that weren’t corrupted as the MacBook was an aluminum model (MacBook Pro) and had more natural shielding than the plastic bodied HP. 
I hope you gave Yvonne crap for not externally backing up her photos.

author: @MarcuccioDaBest
text:
I think you really missed the mark on the Pixel here. Based on Yvonne’s actual priorities, a Pixel should have been one of the strongest options: manageable size, great camera, long software support, clean Android experience, and more than enough performance for normal everyday use.

Yes, Tensor isn’t the most powerful chip on paper, but that difference mainly shows up in gaming and other CPU/GPU-heavy workloads. For messaging, navigation, photos, calendars, browsing, and the kind of everyday use she described, it really isn’t much of a drawback. In fact, the cleaner Android interface and lack of some of Samsung’s extra software may have fit her “I just want it to work” attitude very well.

Battery life was another strange point. In everyday-use testing, the Pixel 10 Pro is actually around the same as the S26+ and sometimes does better in things like browsing and video. Samsung’s big advantage shows up mainly when the phone is being pushed hard, especially gaming. Since that clearly isn’t her use case, it seems like another reason the Pixel was discounted more than it should have been.

I also think shopping almost entirely from what happened to be on display at Best Buy made the Android market look much smaller than it really is. There are a lot more good Android options out there.

The S26+ is obviously a good phone, but I don’t think the video really established why it was a better fit for *her* than the Pixel. Based on the requirements she gave, the Pixel deserved a much more serious look.

author: @markiieee
text:
Why were the only choices what you could find in BestBuy? Based on what Yvonne wanted I think there's a number of other options that Linus wouldn't call boring.
I would have suggested a OnePlus 15, I'm biased because I have one but I love it. 7500mah SiliconCarbon battery so it should cover her battery needs, 120W wired charging and 50W wireless charging so even if she can drain the massive battery it can be charged back up really fast. Snapdragon 8 elite gen 5 and 12GB RAM so plenty of performance, I've had no performance issues at all. OxygenOS is very apple-like so if she likes how the iPhone felt maybe the OnePlus is a good halfway point. 
It doesn't have the greatest camera ever and the AI upscaling can be a bit aggressive at times but for things like family photos it's great. It may not impress photography nerds but my phone is the preferred camera by my family and friends in social situations, the portrait mode is great.

And rather than go to BestBuy, but direct from OnePlus and you get a free gift, I got a new OnePlus watch 3 for free with the phone and it cost a lot less than the S26.

And that's just one other option but to be honest, why not just show Yvonne a compilation of clips from ShortCircuit phone reviews? Wouldn't that give her more of the information she wants?

text:
I really appreciate that this was a full story-arc video.

I completely understand having a setup video with a follow up video a few days or weeks later, and that can absolutely work really we in both the creator and audience's favour, but when Linus said Yvonne was going away for a few weeks, I immediately thought that was the end and we weren't going to get that punch line for the end of the video.

When I popped up the timeline and saw that there was still a decent chunk to go still and that we were going to hear the rest of the story, I honestly felt relieved and grateful. 

I understand in the grand picture it doesn't really matter as at the end of the day with these things, we all have our own opinions of the products we buy, but with the whole video building up a picture of what Yvonne was looking for in a phone, it felt right that we got a true summarisation at the end, so to Linus, Yvonne, Elijah, Emily, Et al, thank you.

author: @EliotHochberg
text:
Bad news: it doesn't matter what phone or platform you use, you can lose all of your photos.

My wife uses WhatsApp, there were a bunch of photos in there that were not saved to her phone, and when she moved to iOS, a weird thing happened when she changed the number, and everything that was there was deleted. She said she didn't care, and maybe not, but it pissed me off.

I suppose the moral of this whole thing is, unless you have really good data hygiene and back up locally to more than one place, with one of those places offsite, at some point you're going to lose some of your data. You cannot depend on cloud services to back things up. Even Google can delete things. I had backed up all of my texts, but apparently there was some change that happen, and you had to click an additional button to retain things past a certain amount of time for an extra fee. So I lost a lot of business texts that I thought I was keeping. Not to mention back up is not working because it decides that you don't have sufficient connectivity and it fails to notify you.

text:
13:45
The Android Ecosystem is STILL very vibrant - just not in north america! 
In the EU, it's totally fair game if you pick Oppo, Vivio, Xiaomi, Motorola or even the often still flying around ZTE devices. Stores near me sell Fairphones on the floor, have Nubia budget options and there even used to be OnePlus. My mother has gotten an Oppo phone as her latest and loves it. I'm heavily considering a Xiaomi or Poco phone and I still have the choice for Pixel, Galaxy and iPhone. 
The issue isn't the android market, the issue is regulations, carrier limitations and fearmongering.
Yes, not everything "china" is safe data wise or transparent in the way the companies operate, but if that's really the issue, instead of rightout banning them, making attempts at regulation for data security and open systems would make much much more sense. But it seems that the big crops, especially Google and Apple, really have a big interest in being "protective" as they're the american "native" phone brands still left as the big players in your region. author: @RainesExtras
text:
Honestly, iCloud is just a mess. I have an iPhone I use as a backup, I am subsribed to iCloud+ so my photo library syncs between all my Apple devices, and on situations where there's not enough storage it can work really well, but Apple is really vague on what's happening behind the scenes.

On that old low storage iPhone I use as a backup, it was behaving really weirdly, photos would say over 20 gigabytes were taking up storage where on my bigger iPhone and other devices it was only like 8. This has happened twice and one thing I did was turn iCloud Photo Library Sync off for just that device but it didn't fix the storage issue, in fact it just made it worse. In my mind I thought clearing the cached files would help but Apple does not offer that option anywhere, so what I did is sign out COMPLETELY off iCloud to the point where Settings would say no Apple Account logged in and Activation Lock was no longer active, and the fact that it doesn't show up in my Apple Account device list. I then went ahead and opened the photo library app, and surprise, my photos were still there, but only like half of it which explains the 20 gig figure (I have 40 gigs of photos on iCloud). I selected all, deleted it, and for some reason even after being signed out of my Apple Account completely, those changes sycned still. I was lucky that Apple was able to recover them because despite the deleted photos not appearing on recently deleted on any of my Apple devices, Apple with their internal tools were able to get them back.

In short, iCloud has always had problems with sync and caching, causing weird storage behaviours that cannot be fixed because they don't give you options to do so, Apple gives you two options, on or off, and there's no way to customise the on feature beyond two toggles they give you and depending on what you want, those toggels can be really broken which results in weird behaviour. Like who would have known that even after signing out of my Apple Account on that phone that iCloud would still sync photo libraries with that phone? It's a mess.

author: @amadtaz
text:
Okay... Now do one where you go into a store and experience what a regular customer would. The vast majority of people who go into a store do not bring a professional tech reviewer with them. There's details you guys miss out on by not being in a store everyday seeing and learning about the minutia of the products and accessories. For example, if you gave the staff the time to show you cases for the phone you picked, you would have been shown/explained the difference between buying a case with magnets and without. You guys clearly bought a case that was not Qi2/MagSafe compatible. Had you known, you guys would have bought the case with magnets so it would actually work well in the car. Something along these lines happens every time you guys do one of these segments and it's annoying. 

Another thing, everything on display in a retail store is planned. Not necessarily planned for the best show floor showcase for customers to experience. But planned the brand paid the store to dedicate that floorspace to showcase that specific product. For example, Sony and the Xperia would need to pay Best Buy $$$$$ and Best Buy would have to invest in that inventory to be on hand for customers. Heck, next time you are in your local Best Buy, you will even notice the flooring being different than the rest of the store because the brand in that zone is responsible for the entire space and its vibes. Best Buy puts the mobile phone section front and center in all of their stores because of the volume of traffic it supplies. Apple and Samsung then duke it out to be at the front of that department with their own bespoke tables and signage installed by their own contractors.

text: As someone who has used Apple’s cloud stuff from the beginning, (early 2000’s) I can tell you that sync problem is something that can happen if the conditions are just right. The images & videos are likely still there in one of their failover backups, so I do have hope that Yvonne will get them back. It may take a bit, but I feel good about it being restored. I pay for the 2 tb iCloud+ tier because I have a Mac and an iPhone (plus older iPhones no longer with cell use) so that’s what makes sense for me. I also have a 4 tb raid 1 NAS that I’m setting up for automatic backing up. I think the backup thing is another (sadly hard learned) lesson that single cloud backups are not 100% reliable. author: @UltravioletMind
text:
Im pretty sure I know EXACTLY what happened, happened to me. you see apple secretly "backs up"  your photos and deletes them from your phone . it replaces them with low quality versions. 
you never really notice because the full quality gets downloaded when you open up and it starts with the oldest.  this happens over a long period of time after an ios update, till eventually your most recent photos start getting backed up and you notice the little delay of the the full quality popping in or you get notified that your storage might be getting full. so you go to investigate and you realise oh wait, i have space on my phone, i dont need icloud storage . Thats when they get you ! if you turn off icloud storage, all the photos get deleted across all your devices! they dissappear from your gallery because they were not the real version but a low quality thumbnail. so you gotta keep icloud on, manually download your thousands of photos individually. Thats the second gotcha.  there's never enough space to download your photos back. you see, because the previous photos were only thumbnails you end up taking photos and recording videos without running into issues. but after turning off icloud now you need more storage to get back the photos you already had. not only that, it also forces you to download everything from icloud not just photos, so your device needs even more space.! 

the only solution is to keep icloud on. download your images in batches, offload them to an external device not connected to icloud(theres another gotcha coming ). once all your media is downloaded , yo u can safely turn off icloud. If your backup device is using apple photos, deleting them from icloud will delete your backups as well for the final gotcha. 
its a horrible hostage situation apple has setup. they delete your images without permission and make it unreasonably difficult to get back. it honestly should be illegal.
